mcq.q: What is the central claim of Sweller (1988)?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Discovery learning always speeds up schema formation in novices
Some forms of problem solving (means-ends) interfere with schema learning
Solving many conventional problems is the fastest way to learn schemas
Experts solve better thanks to stronger general strategies
mcq.e: The abstract: the reason problem solving is ineffective as a learning device is that the cognitive processes of the two activities overlap insufficiently, and means-ends analysis takes processing capacity that is then unavailable for schema acquisition.

mcq.q: According to Sweller (1988), what mainly distinguishes experts from novices in problem solving?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Their ability to search more widely in the problem space
Domain-specific knowledge in the form of schemas
The speed of their short-term memory processing
The number of general problem-solving strategies they know
mcq.e: "domain specific knowledge in the form of schemes is the primary factor distinguishing experts from novices in problem-solving skill."

mcq.q: What did De Groot (1966) find distinguishing chess masters from weaker players?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Only memory for real board positions
Masters searched more moves at each position
Masters recalled even random positions better than novices
Masters calculated many more moves ahead
mcq.e: De Groot found no difference in breadth or depth of search. Chase and Simon (1973): the advantage disappeared for random positions, so it was not general short-term memory.

mcq.q: According to Chase and Simon (1973), how did masters and novices differ in recalling positions?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: The number of chunks was about equal
Novices recalled in larger chunks than masters
Masters recalled single pieces better, novices recalled in chunks
Masters had more chunks but each was the same size
mcq.e: Both recalled in chunks and the number did not differ appreciably; the difference was chunk size: masters' chunks were far larger.

mcq.q: In the physics studies (Larkin et al.; Simon & Simon), how did novices and experts solve problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Both worked backward from the goal with the same strategy
Novices worked backward from the goal then forward
Novices worked forward from the givens; experts worked backward from the goal
Novices tried equations at random; experts looked formulas up in books
mcq.e: Novices used means-ends: set subgoals backward, then work forward; experts chose an equation that let them compute an unknown, because they recognized the problem.

mcq.q: In Chi, Glaser and Rees (1982), how did experts and novices categorize physics problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Both by how difficult they subjectively judged each problem to be
Experts by the principle of solution (such as conservation of energy)
Experts by surface objects in the statement; novices by the principle of solution
Both by the length of the problem statement and the number of givens
mcq.e: Experts grouped problems using the same principle together; novices grouped by surface features such as "inclined plane".

mcq.q: How does Sweller (1988) define a "schema"?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: A model of sensory memory holding the image of the problem for a few seconds
A detailed plan that the solver builds before starting to solve anything
A list of formulas memorized in advance for each particular type of problem
A structure that lets a solver recognize a problem state as one requiring particular moves
mcq.e: "a schema is defined as a structure which allows problem solvers to recognize a problem state as belonging to a particular category of problem states that normally require particular moves."

mcq.q: What does a "transformation problem" (Greeno 1978) consist of?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: A statement, hints and a solution
An initial state, a goal state
Goals, resources and a deadline
Givens, unknowns, and a model answer
mcq.e: Sweller (1988): most maths and maths-related problems are of this kind (initial state, goal state, legal operators) and can be solved by search such as means-ends analysis.

mcq.q: What is means-ends analysis?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Recalling the exact solution to a similar problem seen before
Trying available operators at random until the answer appears
Trying to reduce the difference between the current state
Splitting the problem into identical smaller problems
mcq.e: Means-ends analysis is "attempting to reduce differences between each problem state encountered and the goal state using the operators."

mcq.q: Why does means-ends analysis take so much processing capacity, according to Sweller (1988)?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: The solver must write the solution in a fixed format and check each line
The solver must hold the current state, goal, their relation, operators
The solver must do many large multiplications and divisions
The solver must memorize every equation before making a move
mcq.e: If subgoals are used a goal stack must also be maintained; the capacity needed may be so large that little remains for schema acquisition even if the problem is solved.

mcq.q: What two mechanisms does Sweller (1988) give for why means-ends interferes with learning?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: The learner's native language and their reading speed on the problem text
Learner motivation and the actual difficulty of each problem being solved
Selective attention and limited cognitive processing capacity
Sensory memory and long-term memory as they act during the solving
mcq.e: The two are related: when all capacity is devoted to goal attainment, attention is also devoted to the goal, excluding features needed for schema acquisition.

mcq.q: What is a "nonspecific goal" (goal-free) problem in Sweller (1988)?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: A problem whose specific goal is replaced by "calculate as many variables as you can"
A problem that gives no starting givens at all to the solver
A problem with only the answer printed and everything else left to the solver
A problem with several specific goals that must all be reached at once
mcq.e: For example, "What is the racing car's acceleration?" becomes "Calculate the value of as many variables as you can." This removes the possibility of means-ends.

mcq.q: What did Sweller and Levine (1982) show with maze problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: There was no difference between the two conditions
Maze solvers always found the goal even without knowing its position
Knowing the goal position helped people learn the maze structure faster
Given a known goal position, people often failed to learn the structure
mcq.e: An unknown goal makes means-ends unusable, and people quickly grasped the maze's structure.

mcq.q: What was the result of Sweller, Mawer and Ward (1983) with physics and geometry problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: The goal-free group was faster but only on physics, not on geometry problems
The two groups developed expertise at the same speed across many experiments
The goal-free group developed problem-solving expertise faster than the conventional group
The conventional group developed problem-solving expertise faster than the goal-free group
mcq.e: Across experiments, reducing goal specificity helped expertise develop faster.

mcq.q: Which language was Sweller's (1988) computational model written in, and for what purpose?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Pascal, to simulate long-term memory
LISP, to teach recursion to students
Python, to automatically grade students' work
The production-system language PRISM
mcq.e: A "minimal" production-system model to obtain a relative indicator of the capacity each strategy needs.

mcq.q: What four measures of load did Sweller's (1988) production-system model use?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Symbols, formulas, lines and pages needed per solution
Reaction time, errors, heart rate, pupil dilation
Test score, number of problems, study time, self-confidence
Statements in working memory, productions, cycles
mcq.e: (1) statements in working memory, (2) number of productions, (3) cycles to solution, (4) total number of conditions matched.

mcq.q: What did Table 2 of Sweller (1988) give for active productions in the conventional vs goal-free 3-step problem?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: 4 active productions vs 1 (conventional and goal-free)
10 active productions vs 2 (conventional and goal-free)
4 active productions in both conditions
1 active production vs 4 (conventional and goal-free)
mcq.e: Table 2: active productions 4 vs 1; cycles 5 vs 3; conditions matched 29 vs 17; mean working-memory statements 15.5 vs 14.

mcq.q: What did Table 2 give for cycles and total conditions matched?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Cycles 5 and 3; conditions matched 29 and 17 (conventional and goal-free)
Cycles 3 and 5; conditions matched 17 and 29 (conventional and goal-free)
Cycles 10 and 2; conditions matched 40 and 12
Cycles 14 and 14; conditions matched 14 and 14
mcq.e: Both conditions start with 14 working-memory statements (the goal variable is an extra unknown in goal-free); the conventional one is heavier on every other measure.

mcq.q: What did Owen and Sweller (1985) find about mathematical errors in trigonometry problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: The goal-free group made 4 to 6 times as many mathematical errors per side
Both groups made the same number of mathematical errors per side calculated
The conventional group made 4 to 6 times as many mathematical errors per side calculated
The conventional group made only about 10% more errors per side than the other
mcq.e: The conventional group also found fewer sides yet made more errors in total; the goal-free advantage carried over to later problems (fewer errors, faster).

mcq.q: What were the participants of Sweller's (1988) dual-task experiment?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: 309 eleventh graders, two groups of 154 and 155
24 Year-10 students in Sydney, two groups of 12
75 ninth graders, two groups of 37 and 38
60 first-year university students, two groups of 30
mcq.e: 24 Year-10 students (aged 15–16) from a Sydney high school; a conventional group and a nonspecific-goal group of 12 each.

mcq.q: What was the secondary task in the dual-task experiment?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Solving another trigonometry problem in parallel
Pressing a button on hearing a random click
Counting backward from 100 while solving
Accurately reproducing the diagram
mcq.e: Reproducing the diagram and solution of the preceding problem is an indicator of schema acquisition; six problems, reproduction after problems 2 to 6.

mcq.q: What did the reproduction errors show in the dual-task experiment?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: Only segment-labelling and angle-value errors differed between groups
The conventional group made fewer errors of every kind
The two groups made identical reproduction errors on all six criteria
The nonspecific-goal group made fewer angle-position, side-value
mcq.e: Mann-Whitney: fewer on angle-position (U = 29), side-value (U = 27), side-position (U = 41), solution (U = 17.5); no difference on segment-label (U = 55) and angle-value (U = 63).

mcq.q: Which opposing hypothesis did Sweller (1988) pose for the secondary task?
mcq.sec: Sweller 1988: argument and background
o: High load only speeds up solving without affecting accuracy at all
High load in the primary task might improve memory by strengthening the elements
The secondary task is fully independent of the primary task in every way
High load in the primary task always lowers memory in the secondary task
mcq.e: Two opposing hypotheses: high load lowers secondary-task performance (Sweller's), or it strengthens the elements so secondary performance rises. The data favoured the first.

mcq.q: What does Sweller 1998 tie working memory to about consciousness?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Working memory works outside awareness, like long-term memory
Working memory holds only visual information
Working memory can be equated with consciousness
Working memory stores everything learned, and we are aware of all of it
mcq.e: "Working memory can be equated with consciousness. Humans are conscious of and can monitor only the contents of working memory."

mcq.q: What do Miller (1956) and the estimate for processing (not just holding) in Sweller 1998 say?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Hold about seven items and process exactly seven at once as when merely storing
Hold about seven items, but process only two or three at a time
Hold about three items, but process seven items at a time when comparing
Hold and process about twelve items at the same moment in any task
mcq.e: "Working memory is capable of holding only about seven items... humans are probably only able to deal with two or three items of information simultaneously when required to process."

mcq.q: What does Sweller 1998 use Baddeley for in describing working memory?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: A phonological loop for auditory material
A single processor for all kinds of information
A separate processor for smell and taste
A sensory memory that replaces working memory
mcq.e: Two systems governed by a central executive; using both channels raises effective capacity (less than additively), the basis of the modality effect.

mcq.q: According to Sweller 1998, where does intellectual skill mainly reside?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: In long-term memory, as schemas of varying degrees of automation
In sensory memory, through faster processing of what the senses take in
In reading speed and the short-term recall capacity each person is born with
In working memory, through long complex chains of reasoning kept in mind
mcq.e: "The seat of human intellectual skill may more likely reside in long-term rather than working memory."

mcq.q: How many configurations did Simon and Gilmartin (1973) estimate a master learns?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: About 10,000
About 1,000
About 100,000
mcq.e: Sweller 1998 cites the estimate of "as many as 100,000 such configurations".

mcq.q: What are the two functions of schema construction in Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Doubling working-memory capacity, and speeding up reading
Storing and organizing information in long-term memory
Filtering false information, and detecting others' errors
Reducing what has to be learned, and increasing test items
mcq.e: "schema construction has two functions: the storage and organization of information in long-term memory and a reduction of working memory load."

mcq.q: What does the "restaurant schema" example in Sweller 1998 illustrate?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: A schema containing a lot of information still takes up the space of one element
Restaurants are a prime example of content with very high intrinsic load for novices
Novices grasp the restaurant concept more easily than experts because they know less
Working memory can hold thousands of independent elements if they are grouped
mcq.e: The restaurant schema includes food, money, buildings, furniture... but can be held as a single entity so we find it easy.

mcq.q: What is automation in Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Stopping conscious processing because the body is tired and needs rest
Processing faster with the help of a computer or some other automatic tool
Memorizing a long passage word for word after many days of repetition
Processing that largely bypasses working memory after extensive practice
mcq.e: After extensive practice a procedure can be run with little conscious effort (for example adults read without processing individual letters).

mcq.q: What did Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon (1985) show about isomorphic problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Difficulty differed at most twofold, due to statement length
Difficulty could differ by a factor of 16
Difficulty cannot be reduced even by learning the rules first
Isomorphic problems always have the same difficulty
mcq.e: Having solvers memorize the unfamiliar rules first reduced the gap considerably; initial attempts may have served only to automate the rules.

mcq.q: What does Sweller 1998's example (a + b)/c = d, solve for a, illustrate?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Novices solve faster because they do not need to recall any step
The problem is too complex for anyone, even those with automated schemas
It is an example of extraneous load due to poor presentation
Someone with an automated schema knows at once to multiply through
mcq.e: A learner with the schema knows the first move automatically; one who has just learned it must ask "do I multiply the denominator or subtract the addend?", using capacity.

mcq.q: According to Sweller 1998, what does intrinsic load depend on?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Only the attractiveness of images and colours in the material
Only the length of the material and pages to read per session
Only the time the lecturer spends and the number of exercises
The number of elements processed at once
mcq.e: "Intrinsic cognitive load through element interactivity is determined by an interaction between the nature of the material being learned and the expertise of the learners."

mcq.q: Why is learning foreign-language vocabulary (Fe = iron, Cu = copper) low in intrinsic load despite many items?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Learning vocabulary does not use working memory at all, only long-term memory
Vocabulary is stored directly in sensory memory so needs no working memory
Each element can be learned on its own without reference to the others
Vocabulary is always easier to remember than any other content
mcq.e: Low element interactivity: elements can be learned one by one, so intrinsic load is low despite large numbers.

mcq.q: Why does the word order "all of the" (right) and "of all the" (wrong) count as high intrinsic load?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Because children can learn only single words, not word order
Because the phrase is rare in English so learners seldom meet it
Because grammar is always harder than vocabulary for every learner
It cannot be learned word by word; the words
mcq.e: Sweller 1998: learning word order is high element interactivity; considering one word at a time makes no sense.

mcq.q: For a/b = c becoming a = cb, what consequence of rote-learning "move b across as cb" does Sweller 1998 note?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Load drops but at the expense of understanding of the procedure
Load rises but understanding of the procedure is left completely unchanged
No effect on load and no effect on understanding of the procedure either
Load rises but at the same time understanding of the procedure rises too
mcq.e: Learning the procedure by rote lowers load "at the expense of understanding".

mcq.q: When is the word "understanding" used, according to Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: When the learner gets full marks on a test
When the material consists only of isolated facts
When the material is high in element interactivity
When the learner remembers every detail exactly
mcq.e: We speak of remembering or forgetting a translation of "cat"; getting the transformation a/b = c wrong we call failing to understand.

mcq.q: Why can element interactivity not be determined from the material alone?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Many interacting elements for one person may be a single element for an expert
Learning material is always written by experts
Element interactivity is fixed for every learner, whatever their prior knowledge
The longer the material, the lower the element interactivity
mcq.e: You must count the interacting elements handled by people at a given level of expertise; hence learner analysis accompanies content analysis.

mcq.q: What is extraneous load in Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Load from the learner's motivation, which varies with individual interest
Load from useful effort spent building schemas, which should always be maximized
Unnecessary load from how material is presented or what activities are required
Load from the real complexity of the content, which design cannot alter
mcq.e: "Extraneous cognitive load is unnecessary cognitive load and can be altered by instructional interventions."

mcq.q: How does germane load differ from extraneous load?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Germane is intrinsic and extraneous is germane; they differ only in name
Both are always harmful for learning
Both are alterable by design, but germane contributes to schema building
Germane load cannot be altered, extraneous load can
mcq.e: Extraneous load reflects effort on poorly designed instruction; germane load reflects effort that builds schemas. Good design lowers extraneous and raises germane load.

mcq.q: How does Sweller 1998 describe the relation between intrinsic and extraneous load?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: They are independent of each other, so their sum does not matter at all
They are additive; high intrinsic plus high extraneous can be harmful to learning
They cancel each other, so high load of one lowers the load of the other
They multiply, so one of them being low is enough for learning to be safe
mcq.e: "Intrinsic cognitive load due to element interactivity and extraneous cognitive load due to instructional design are additive."

mcq.q: When intrinsic load is low, what does high extraneous load do, per Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: It always causes severe overload, exactly as when intrinsic load is high
It may do little harm because the total stays within working-memory limits
It always raises germane load correspondingly, because learners try harder
It always raises intrinsic load by the same amount as the extraneous load
mcq.e: For example split attention is no problem for low-intrinsic-load material; it matters only when element interactivity is high.

mcq.q: According to Sweller 1998, when should germane load be raised?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Only when intrinsic load is extremely high and extraneous load is also high
Only for learners who already have a great deal of experience with the topic
At all times, whether the learner's total load is low or already very high
When the sum of intrinsic, extraneous and germane load still fits within working-memory limits
mcq.e: It works only if the total "stays within working memory limits"; the method is to cut extraneous load and redirect attention to building schemas.

mcq.q: Which example does Sweller 1998 give for raising germane load when studying worked examples?
mcq.sec: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998: architecture and kinds of load
o: Remove all examples so that learners must work everything out from scratch
Ask questions about examples or make them incomplete
Give examples with the answers printed on the next page for checking
Shorten each example to a single line of summary that can be read quickly
mcq.e: Students often skip worked examples; procedures such as asking questions or incomplete examples make them process them and build schemas.

mcq.q: How do mental load and mental effort differ in Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Load is the test score while effort is the time spent studying
Load is imposed by the task; effort is the resources actually allocated
Load is chosen by the learner while effort is imposed by the teacher
Load exists only in novices while effort exists only in experts
mcq.e: Mental load: task demands; mental effort: the capacity actually allocated; performance is the outcome.

mcq.q: Why do scores alone not fully reveal cognitive load (Sweller 1998)?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Scores are always marked wrongly because raters lack training
Learners can raise effort to compensate
Scores measure only motivation, not cognitive capacity
Cognitive load has nothing to do with the task assigned
mcq.e: Within capacity limits, students can compensate for higher mental load by investing more mental effort, so effort should be measured.

mcq.q: What three categories of measuring mental effort does Sweller 1998 give?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Multiple-choice, essay and oral tests
Entrance test, midterm and final exam in one course
Subjective (self-rating), physiological
Direct observation, in-depth interview and questionnaire survey
mcq.e: After Wierwille and Eggemeier (1993): subjective, physiological, and task- and performance-based (primary and secondary tasks).

mcq.q: What is the common subjective scale in Sweller 1998, and what are its labels?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: A 10-point scale from "0 points" to "10 points"
A 7-point scale from "completely false" to "completely true"
A 5-point scale from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree"
A 9-point scale from "very, very low mental effort" to "very
mcq.e: Paas's (1992) 9-point scale based on Bratfisch, Borg and Dornic (1972). Marcus, Cooper and Sweller (1996) and others used a 7-point version.

mcq.q: How did Paas, van Merriënboer and Adam (1994) evaluate subjective scales and heart-rate measures?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: The subjective scale was sensitive, reliable, valid and non-intrusive
Both were equally sensitive, reliable and valid; heart rate was even more objective
Both were unreliable and invalid, so the authors advised against both
Heart rate beat the subjective scale on every criterion
mcq.e: Conclusion: subjective rating is the most promising technique; spectral analysis of heart-rate variability is non-intrusive but unreliable, invalid and sensitive only to large differences.

mcq.q: How do Paas and van Merriënboer (1993) compute instructional efficiency?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Divide the test score by the total study time of each person
Convert mental effort and performance to z-scores
Subtract errors from correct answers and rescale to 0–100
Subtract confidence from actual score and plot in a four-cell grid
mcq.e: It combines the intensity of effort with the level of performance; a point is in "High Efficiency" when performance is high and effort low.

mcq.q: What did the efficiency results in Paas and van Merriënboer (1994a) in geometry show?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Worked examples were efficient only under low variability
There was no difference in efficiency between the two conditions
The worked-example condition was more efficient than the conventional-problem condition
The conventional-problem condition was more efficient than the worked-example condition
mcq.e: Worked examples led to better schema construction and higher efficiency than conventional problems.

mcq.q: Which example presents the goal-free effect in Sweller 1998?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: A car moves at a steady 60 km/h for two hours: find the distance travelled
A car brakes on a wet road: find the friction force acting on its wheels
A car accelerates uniformly from rest for 1 minute to 2 km/min: calculate as many variables as you can
An object falls freely from 100 m: find the time it takes to fall
mcq.e: The conventional version asks "How far has it traveled?"; the goal-free version says "Calculate the value of as many variables as you can", yet the same values and equations result.

mcq.q: How do the cognitive processes differ in goal-free versus means-ends even though the results are the same?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: More subgoals must be held so no unknown is missed
Every state must be compared with the goal at each step
No operator or equation is used because the answer follows from the statement
Only the current state and applicable operators must be held, not the goal
mcq.e: Sweller 1998: goal-free requires only a state and any operator that applies, exactly the combination needed for schema construction.

mcq.q: What do Bobis, Sweller and Cooper (1994) and Ayres (1993) show, per Sweller 1998, about goal-free?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: The effect vanishes when the goal model is placed in front of the students in paper folding
The effect occurs only in university math
The effect occurs only with homework, not in class
The effect occurs in primary-school paper folding and in geometry
mcq.e: Bobis: paper folding with the final model absent, analogous to a missing goal; Ayres: most errors in the subgoal phase, fewer for goal-free.

mcq.q: What counterintuitive prediction does the worked-example effect in Sweller 1998 make?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Worked examples work only once learners are already good at the topic
Solving problems always beats studying worked examples because learners must think harder
Studying worked examples can beat actually solving the equivalent problems
Worked examples raise extraneous load compared with solving the same problems
mcq.e: Worked examples eliminate search and focus attention on states and operators, so extraneous load is low.

mcq.q: What did Zhu and Simon (1987) report about worked examples?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: A two-year math course had to be stretched to three years to fit examples
Worked examples helped only in foreign-language courses, not in mathematics
Worked examples did not shorten any course, as students still needed to solve problems
A three-year math course was completed in two years by stressing worked examples
mcq.e: In long-term studies worked examples could replace conventional classroom teaching.

mcq.q: What did Paas (1992) find about showing examples to students who failed?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: The conventional group transferred better when they saw examples
The two groups did not differ in transfer
Even with a chance to study examples
The worked-example group transferred worse than the conventional group
mcq.e: A possible explanation: the failed solutions were incorporated into the constructed schemas.

mcq.q: What did Trafton and Reiser (1993) show with LISP?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: College students learned more after solving problems than after studying equivalent examples
Only final-year students benefited from worked examples in LISP
College students learned more after studying worked examples than after solving equivalent problems
Worked examples did not help students learn programming
mcq.e: This is evidence in the programming domain: worked examples beat solving equivalent problems for learning LISP.

mcq.q: What disadvantage of worked examples does Sweller 1998 note?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Worked examples always cause extraneous overload in every learner
Worked examples make learners forget schemas they already have
Worked examples cannot be used in math or programming
Lack of genuine problem solving may reduce motivation
mcq.e: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993): heavy use of worked examples can give stereotyped solution patterns. Hence goal-free and completion problems as alternatives.

mcq.q: What is a completion problem (Van Merriënboer and Krammer)?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: A problem with a full solution to read and copy exactly
A problem giving a state, the goal
A problem giving only the final answer with no statement or solution
A problem with no solution and no specific goal for free exploration
mcq.e: A worked example is a completion problem with a full solution; a conventional problem is one with no solution.

mcq.q: What is the completion strategy?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Starting with nearly complete problems and gradually moving to ones where learners generate most of the solution
Using only fully blank problems throughout the course so learners do every step alone
Using only fully worked problems throughout the course so learners always have a model
Starting with blank problems and gradually adding worked solutions until all have full solutions
mcq.e: From little completion to much completion: handing responsibility to the learner gradually.

mcq.q: In which subject and with what result did Van Merriënboer (1990) study completion problems?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Physics in 5 lessons: the two groups were equal on new transfer problems
English in 10 lessons: the completion group was worse at writing new paragraphs
A ten-lesson introductory programming course: the completion group beat the conventional group on building new programs
Algebra in 3 lessons: the conventional group beat the completion group at new equations
mcq.e: The completion group modified and extended existing programs, the other designed and coded new ones; analysis showed completion encouraged the use of programming templates.

mcq.q: What did Van Merriënboer and de Croock (1992) log files show for programming students?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: There was no difference in how the two groups looked for information
Conventional-problem students had to search for useful examples
Completion students had to search for more examples because the program lacked information
Conventional students needed no documents or examples as they remembered every template
mcq.e: That is why completion lowers extraneous load: the information is in the task.

mcq.q: What drawback of completion problems does Sweller 1998 note?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: They take time to design and require many decisions about which part to give
They always raise extraneous load relative to conventional problems
They can be used only by highly expert learners
They always lower long-term motivation because they are easier than conventional problems
mcq.e: The designer must consider which part of the solution to present and which to leave; a good completion problem requires understanding the partial solution and a nontrivial completion.

mcq.q: When does the split-attention effect arise?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: When information has a single source but is presented too briefly to read
When both sources are self-contained and simply repeat the same content
When two sources of information must be integrated mentally before they make sense
When information is presented in speech rather than in writing on screen
mcq.e: A geometry diagram and its solution statements are meaningless alone; physical integration reduces extraneous load.

mcq.q: What did Tarmizi and Sweller (1988) find with geometry examples?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Only integrated examples beat both split examples and conventional problems
Conventional problems beat every type of worked example
Integrated and split examples gave equal results, both beating conventional problems
Only split examples beat both integrated examples and conventional problems
mcq.e: The worked-example effect appeared only with integrated examples: evidence for both split-attention and worked-example effects.

mcq.q: What did Sweller and Chandler (1994) show about learning a computer application?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Learning was better with a structured manual
Computers always help learning and manuals are not needed
No difference between the two learning conditions
Learning was better with both manual and computer in use side by side
mcq.e: Only with high element interactivity material. Cerpa, Chandler and Sweller (1996): putting everything on screen worked as well; the problem was split attention between screen and manual, not the computer.

mcq.q: When does split attention clearly hurt?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: When content has high element interactivity
When material is text only with no diagrams
When learners are already experts
When content has low element interactivity
mcq.e: The first evidence for the importance of intrinsic load alongside extraneous load.

mcq.q: Under what condition does the modality effect arise?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: From redundancy, when the same information is repeated in two different ways
From worked examples, when learners solve a problem themselves without help
From split attention, when text is spoken rather than shown as written text
From variability, when practice uses many different kinds of problems
mcq.e: Mousavi, Low and Sweller (1995): a visual diagram plus spoken text beat diagram plus written text in geometry; Tindall-Ford et al. (1997) replicated it with electrical engineering.

mcq.q: What did Tindall-Ford, Chandler and Sweller (1997) find about the modality effect?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: It appeared in no condition, as the two did not differ
It appeared only with high element interactivity material
It appeared with all material, even low element interactivity
It appeared only with low element interactivity
mcq.e: Efficiency computed from load and performance also favoured audio/visual only under high element interactivity.

mcq.q: When does the redundancy effect occur?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: When information is presented too sparsely
When learners have no prior knowledge
When sources must be integrated mentally to be understood
When sources are each self-contained
mcq.e: If integration is needed, it reduces load; if each source is intelligible, integration can increase load, so remove the redundant part.

mcq.q: What does Chandler and Sweller's (1991) heart-and-lungs blood-flow diagram illustrate?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: A diagram cannot show blood flow, only written labels can describe it
Written labels always improve learning for every kind of material shown
A diagram always needs written labels in order to be understood at all
Text repeating what an arrowed diagram already shows clearly is redundant
mcq.e: Because the diagram could be understood alone, statements like "Blood from the lungs flows into the left atrium" were redundant.

mcq.q: What did Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1998) show with electrical apprentices?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: The description was always needed for every electrician, even experts
The diagram was always redundant and text alone sufficed
For novices the description was needed and should be integrated
The description was always redundant for every electrician and should be removed at the start
mcq.e: "material that is redundant for some learners and so best eliminated, may be essential for less experienced learners and best integrated." (An early form of expertise reversal.)

mcq.q: How does Sweller 1998 use McNamara, Kintsch, Songer and Kintsch (1996)?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Adding coherence detail helped low-knowledge readers
Adding coherence detail helped only high-knowledge readers, not low
Adding coherence detail helped all readers equally, whatever their knowledge
Adding coherence detail hindered all readers equally, whatever their knowledge
mcq.e: High-knowledge readers had to process actively with the less coherent text; the additions may have been redundant for them.

mcq.q: Why was the redundancy effect "discovered, forgotten and rediscovered" (Sweller 1998)?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Because the effect appears only in the laboratory and vanishes in real classrooms
Because the effect is always tiny and researchers simply ignored it
Because it is counterintuitive and was not placed in a detailed theoretical framework
Because no experiment could replicate the effect over the decades
mcq.e: Many people believe redundancy is at worst neutral; it is hard to accept that it has negative consequences. No work shows advantages of redundancy unless the base material was very poor.

mcq.q: What does the variability effect mean?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Practising varied versions of a task improves transfer
Practice ordered from easy to hard is always best
Practising exactly the same type of problem is best for transfer
Practice reduces cognitive load at every stage
mcq.e: Quilici and Mayer (1996): example sets varying the surface story for the same structure helped categorize statistics word problems better.

mcq.q: What is the "transfer paradox"?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Transfer happens only when cognitive load is very low, so avoid all difficulty
Instruction that improves transfer always lowers load during practice and shortens learning
Instruction that improves transfer often raises load during practice or needs more time
Transfer always happens without practice because learners infer applications
mcq.e: Variability raised cognitive load during learning yet improved transfer, seeming to contradict CLT; the explanation: germane load rose.

mcq.q: How did Paas and van Merriënboer (1994a) interpret variability within CLT?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Variability helps in all learning conditions whether extraneous load is high or low
Variability is always harmful because it raises cognitive load during practice
Variability helps only with conventional problems, not with worked examples
Variability helps only when extraneous load is low, as with worked examples
mcq.e: A significant interaction between problem format and variability: only worked examples plus high variability gave good transfer.

mcq.q: What does Sweller 1998 say about ordering exercises from simple to complex?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: It is optimal at every level of intrinsic load because it lowers extraneous and raises germane
It may prevent overload but neither lowers extraneous load nor raises germane load
It always raises extraneous load because learners must readjust each time
It always raises germane load because learners progress gradually from easy to hard
mcq.e: Except under very high intrinsic load. CLT predicts better learning from formats that lower extraneous load plus more random sequences that raise germane load; being tested with CASCO (teaching programming).

mcq.q: What conclusion does Sweller 1998 draw about split attention, redundancy and modality under low element interactivity?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Only positive consequences under low element interactivity because learners get extra sources
No conclusion can be drawn because experiments conflict in every condition
No appreciable negative consequences under low element interactivity
Major negative consequences at every level of element interactivity, even for simple content
mcq.e: Extraneous load matters only when element interactivity is high.

mcq.q: Which future directions does the conclusion of Sweller 1998 name?
mcq.sec: Sweller et al. 1998: measuring load and the effects
o: Focus entirely on physiological measurement because subjective scales are unreliable
Germane load will be a major focus; and applications for groups with impaired cognitive capacity such as older adults
Study only primary-school pupils because other groups do not differ from them
End CLT research because the evidence is already sufficient for every effect
mcq.e: The authors expect progress on germane load; age-related declines may be compensated by more capacity-efficient design.

mcq.q: How do Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) define "learning"?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: An increase in the number of exercises completed in class
A change in long-term memory
The formation of a positive attitude to the subject
A change in scores between two consecutive exams
mcq.e: "Learning, in turn, is defined as a change in long-term memory." If nothing has changed in long-term memory, nothing has been learned.

mcq.q: How is "direct instructional guidance" defined?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Information that fully explains the concepts
Making students follow the teacher step by step without asking any questions
Giving students the final answers to all exercises so they can check themselves
Lecturing only, leaving all exercises for students to do alone at home
mcq.e: Definition in the opening: "providing information that fully explains the concepts and procedures students are required to learn as well as learning strategy support that is compatible with human cognitive architecture."

mcq.q: What two assumptions underlie minimally guided programs according to the authors?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Students learn best by listening passively and the discipline's procedures do not matter to novices
Students should work alone and knowledge is best learned by being tested often in class
The teacher is the only source of knowledge and students learn best by copying the lecture
Students solve "authentic" problems constructing solutions themselves
mcq.e: "First they challenge students to solve authentic problems... Second, they appear to assume that knowledge can best be acquired through experience based on the procedures of the discipline."

mcq.q: What did Kirschner 2006 cite Peterson and Peterson (1959) for?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Working memory holds only visual information for about five minutes then loses it completely
Working memory holds information for about a week if rehearsed thoroughly
Working memory has no time limit if the learner concentrates intently on the content
Almost all unrehearsed information in working memory is lost within 30 seconds
mcq.e: Kirschner 2006, p.77: the 30-second limit for unrehearsed new information.

mcq.q: What figure did Kirschner 2006 cite from Cowan (2001)?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Capacity may be only about 4 ± 1 elements
Capacity is about 20 elements when the items are meaningful
There is no capacity limit at all for genuinely new information
Capacity is about 7 ± 2 elements, as Miller originally reported
mcq.e: Miller gave about seven, but it may be as low as four plus or minus one (Cowan 2001); when processing, perhaps two or three.

mcq.q: What structure did Ericsson and Kintsch (1995) propose, as mentioned by Kirschner 2006?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Long-term motor memory for physical skills practised for years
Long-term sensory memory for images and sounds just observed
Long-term working memory for familiar, automated information
Short-term long-term memory for new information never seen before
mcq.e: The altered characteristics of working memory when processing familiar vs unfamiliar material led them to propose it.

mcq.q: What does Kirschner 2006 say of constructivism as a description and as an instructional theory?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: It is a correct instructional theory but a wrong description of learning, so use it for the able only
It describes learning accurately, but its instructional consequences do not necessarily follow
It is both a wrong description of learning and a wrong instructional theory, both rejected outright
It is both a correct description and the best instructional theory, and its consequences follow naturally
mcq.e: "The constructivist description of learning is accurate, but the instructional consequences suggested by constructivists do not necessarily follow."

mcq.q: What is the distinction between "teaching a discipline as inquiry" and "teaching it by inquiry" per Kirschner 2006?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: The first emphasizes research processes as content
The first is an effective teaching method and the second is content for beginners to learn
Both are teaching methods suited to novices if a teacher guides them carefully
The two phrases mean the same and the authors use them interchangeably throughout the paper
mcq.e: Confusing the two (Hurd's 1969 "rationale of the scientist") is the major fallacy: novices are not miniature experts.

mcq.q: What historical loop does Mayer (2004) note about discovery learning?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Discovery was never studied again after being rejected in the 1950s
Discovery kept the same name through the decades and most teachers accepted it
Each decade evidence rejects a discovery approach
Each decade discovery gets stronger evidence and keeps its old name
mcq.e: "each time, the evidence has favored a guided approach": discovery, experiential learning, problem-based learning, constructivist instruction.

mcq.q: What did Aulls (2002) observe of teachers implementing constructivist activities?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: There was no difference among teachers since all taught alike in class
The most effective teacher did not interact with students, only handing out materials
The most effective teacher let students discover entirely freely and barely intervened
The most effective teacher spent much time teaching content and providing scaffolding
mcq.e: Kirschner's reading: most teachers implementing constructivism end up providing considerable guidance.

mcq.q: What did Tuovinen and Sweller (1999) show about exploration practice vs worked examples?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Both imposed the same load on all learners, so either choice gave equivalent results
Exploration imposed more load and gave poorer learning
Worked examples imposed more load and gave poorer learning in novices as they had more to read
Exploration imposed less load and gave better learning for all learners, novices and skilled alike
mcq.e: Less knowledgeable learners were harmed by exploration; more knowledgeable ones "did not experience a negative effect and benefited equally from both."

mcq.q: What does Kirschner 2006 say about the worked-example effect as expertise increases?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: It disappears and then reverses
It gets stronger as learners gain experience
It appears only in learners with a lot of experience
It does not change with experience
mcq.e: This is the expertise reversal effect (Kalyuga et al. 2003); problem solving becomes more effective only when learners have enough experience.

mcq.q: Under what conditions does the worked-example effect fail, per Kirschner 2006?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: When examples are presented in integrated form and learners have just started the content
When examples are written in plain language and learners are very young with no experience
When examples carry a step-by-step explanation and learners are at a low level of expertise
When examples are themselves structured to impose heavy load
mcq.e: Examples in a split-attention format can impose as heavy a load as searching for the solution (Tarmizi and Sweller 1988; Ward and Sweller 1990).

mcq.q: What is a process worksheet (Van Merriënboer 1997) and what evidence exists?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: A grading sheet for each test; law students using it did worse than other groups
An attendance sheet; there is no experimental evidence of its effect
A sheet describing the phases of solving with hints for each
A lab-result record; medical students using it did better than other groups
mcq.e: Nadolski, Kirschner and van Merriënboer (2005): law students with a process worksheet produced more coherent and accurate case work.

mcq.q: What common finding in aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) research does Kirschner 2006 cite?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Strong treatments benefit less able learners
Strong treatments are best for all learners, whatever their level or initial ability
Weak treatments are best for all learners because they can explore in their own way
There is no interaction between learner ability and teaching method in ATI studies
mcq.e: Kyllonen and Lajoie (2003): "strong treatments benefited less able learners and weaker treatments benefited more able learners."

mcq.q: What did Clark (1989) find in reviewing about 70 ATI studies?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Low-aptitude students always progressed more in less guided conditions than in guided ones
None of the roughly 70 studies produced findings of note on this matter
High-aptitude students always got worse in conditions with much guidance from the teacher
Low-aptitude students in less guided conditions sometimes scored lower at posttest than at pretest
mcq.e: "Knowing less after instruction": lack of strong learning support can produce a measurable loss for less experienced learners.

mcq.q: What did Clark (1982) report about preference when learners chose more or less guided versions?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: There was no link between preference and outcome
Low-ability learners choosing less guidance often liked it but learned less
High-ability learners choosing less guidance always learned more
Low-ability learners choosing less guidance often hated it and learned more
mcq.e: Liking is not the same as learning; effective components often demand attention-driven effort and so are not liked.

mcq.q: How does Kirschner 2006 assess the Kolb Learning Style Inventory?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: It is firmly validated and widely used because its test-retest reliability is very high in many studies
It has never been studied independently so the authors can offer no comment on the instrument
It has strong predictive validity and high reliability, so the authors advise using it to classify learners
Attempts at validation have been largely unsuccessful: low test-retest reliability
mcq.e: Iliff (1994) meta-analysis of 101 LSI studies: low correlations (< .5), weak to medium effect sizes; Ruble and Stout (1993): low test-retest reliability.

mcq.q: Which results from Albanese and Mitchell's (1993) meta-analysis of medical PBL does Kirschner cite?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: No difference in any outcome between the two training programs compared in the studies
Lower clinical scores, worse residency selection, much lower cost per patient
Lower basic science scores, more study hours a day, more unnecessary tests ordered
Higher basic science scores, fewer study hours a day, fewer unnecessary tests ordered
mcq.e: PBL students had better clinical scores but ordered more tests at higher cost per patient; the higher scores may reflect more time in clinical settings.

mcq.q: What did Colliver (2000) conclude about PBL in medicine?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: No statistical effect on standardized test scores in the first two years; PBL is more costly
PBL cheaper and better than the traditional curriculum on most outcomes measured
PBL worse than the traditional curriculum on standardized tests and costlier on every count
PBL clearly superior on standardized tests in the first two years despite higher training cost
mcq.e: "PBL is not more effective but is more costly than traditional instruction."

mcq.q: What did Arocha and Patel (1995) find about PBL students' reasoning?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: They kept backward reasoning and did not acquire forward reasoning, a hallmark of expertise
There was no difference in reasoning style between PBL and regular-curriculum students
They had better forward reasoning than students from the regular curriculum, even after years of practice
Both forward and backward reasoning were stronger than in students on the regular curriculum
mcq.e: This may relate to working-memory load during problem solving hindering schema acquisition.

mcq.q: What is the final conclusion of Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006)?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: The evidence splits evenly so the authors cannot recommend either approach
Many studies support minimal guidance for novices, including controlled studies
Direct guidance harms novices because they lose the chance to discover for themselves
No research supports minimal guidance; the evidence favours strong direct guidance
mcq.e: "no body of research supporting the technique... controlled studies almost uniformly support direct, strong instructional guidance... of novice to intermediate learners."

mcq.q: Even for learners with considerable prior knowledge, what does Kirschner 2006 say strong guidance is found to be?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Much less effective than unguided approaches
Much more effective than unguided approaches
About as effective as unguided approaches
Impossible to compare with unguided approaches
mcq.e: "Even for students with considerable prior knowledge, strong guidance while learning is most often found to be equally effective as unguided approaches."

mcq.q: What does Hmelo-Silver (2004) suggest for PBL, as quoted?
mcq.sec: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006
o: Use the same PBL model for every age and developmental level with no changes
Remove direct instruction entirely because students must discover everything themselves
Drop supports such as procedural facilitation because they reduce learner autonomy
Tailor it to the learners' developmental level
mcq.e: Quote: "there may be a place for direct instruction on a just-in-time basis... a lecture at the right time may be beneficial."

mcq.q: According to the preface of Sweller, Ayres and Kalyuga (2011), what does CLT comprise?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: Aspects of cognitive architecture relevant to instruction plus the instructional consequences that follow
Only principles for designing software interfaces and the layout of buttons
Only a list of empirical effects with no theoretical basis connecting them
Only a model for measuring load using neuroscience and brain imaging methods
mcq.e: "Cognitive load theory consists of aspects of human cognitive architecture that are relevant to instruction along with the instructional consequences that flow from the architecture."

mcq.q: Into how many parts is the book divided, and what are they?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: Three: theory, experiments and applications, each with six chapters of the book
Five: categories of knowledge, cognitive architecture, categories of load
Two: cognitive architecture and instructional effects, with a short concluding chapter
Four: history, measurement, effects and the future of cognitive load theory
mcq.e: Part I categories of knowledge, Part II human cognitive architecture, Part III categories of cognitive load, Part IV instructional effects, Part V conclusions.

mcq.q: What is "biologically primary knowledge" according to the preface?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: Information humans have evolved to acquire naturally
Information learned at school for cultural reasons that humans have not evolved to acquire naturally
Information only experts hold in each field that cannot be taught to novices
Biological information taught in secondary school in ordinary natural science subjects
mcq.e: Biologically secondary knowledge is what we need for cultural reasons but did not evolve to acquire; educational institutions exist to teach it and CLT deals almost exclusively with it.

mcq.q: Which part of the cognitive model makes CLT stress that "limits disappear"?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: When new information is repeated five times in the same lesson right after being introduced
When the teacher slows down and repeats each important idea at least twice in the lesson
When familiar information is stored in long-term memory, capacity
When the learner has slept enough so working memory is fully restored before the lesson
mcq.e: Preface: limited "if dealing with novel information but unlimited in capacity and duration if dealing with familiar information previously stored in a very large long-term memory."

mcq.q: How are "CLT effects" generated and tested, according to the preface?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: Comparing a new procedure with a common method in randomized controlled experiments
Only by surveying teachers on how satisfied they are with new teaching procedures
Only by reanalysing national exam scores from many years to find general patterns
Only by computer simulation of working-memory activity under many different conditions
mcq.e: When a new procedure beats a common one, a cognitive load effect is demonstrated; Chapters 7 to 17 describe the effects.

mcq.q: Which chapters of the book are said to cover kinds of load and how to measure them?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: Chapter 5 (kinds of load) and Chapter 6 (measurement techniques)
Chapters 17 and 18, on the last effect and the conclusions of the whole book
Chapters 1 and 2, on classifying knowledge and the evolutionary model of cognition
Chapters 10 and 11, on the instructional effects generated by the theory
mcq.e: Part III: Chapter 5 introduces categories of load, their interactions and consequences; Chapter 6 discusses techniques for measuring cognitive load.

mcq.q: How does the preface describe the development of CLT over two to three decades?
mcq.sec: Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga (2011) book
o: New effects sometimes failed to generalize, prompting theory revisions
The effects always generalize perfectly to every field so no adjustment is needed
The theory was abandoned and replaced by another based on social cognition
The theory has not changed since 1988 because the effects all generalized perfectly
mcq.e: "the changes to cognitive load theory have been driven largely by the instructional effects generated by the theory" (a feedback loop).

mcq.q: Why do worked examples and completion tasks suit novice programmers under CLT?
mcq.sec: Link to the thesis
o: They replace writing code entirely so students need no further practice
They reduce needless search, leaving working memory for building schemas
They let students finish without needing to understand the code at all
They raise extraneous load so students work harder on the sample code
mcq.e: Van Merriënboer (1990) and Trafton & Reiser (1993) are evidence in programming. Remember to fade (completion strategy) as students progress.

mcq.q: If AI hands novices complete code from the first question, which CLT prediction is reasonable?
mcq.sec: Link to the thesis
o: More programming schema because students read more code and so understand more deeply
Less load now but less schema-building effort, so it stays hard once AI is removed
Higher extraneous load because AI answers slowly and students wait a long time each time
No effect on learning since complete source code equals writing it yourself in every way
mcq.e: This is an inference from CLT, not a result of the papers; check with a no-AI test (Bastani 2025 in Module 14 supports this direction).

mcq.q: Why measure the 9-point mental-effort scale in the thesis?
mcq.sec: Link to the thesis
o: Because the 9-point scale is compulsory in every education study that uses AI tools
Because the 9-point scale can fully replace the final learning-outcome test for students
Because the 9-point scale directly measures students' real scores without any test being needed
Because scores do not reveal compensatory effort; Kapur 2014 also used it
mcq.e: Sweller 1998 calls the subjective scale the most promising technique; Kapur 2014 (Module 01) used it to compare PF and DI.

mcq.q: What does expertise reversal suggest for adjusting the AI's hint level in a programming class?
mcq.sec: Link to the thesis
o: Keep maximal guidance for every student for the whole semester regardless of level
Gradually reduce guidance as students gain prior knowledge
Remove guidance entirely from the first session so students explore AI use alone
Increase guidance as students get better so they can learn more in a short time
mcq.e: Kalyuga et al. (2001, 2003): worked examples help novices then lose their edge; design for fading.

mcq.q: What does split attention suggest for designing a programming exercise page?
mcq.sec: Link to the thesis
o: Put all explanations at the end of the document to read after the whole code
Put only code with no explanation so students infer each line on their own
Put explanations on a separate page so the exercise stays short and tidy
Put comments and explanations right beside the code lines they concern
mcq.e: Sweller 1998: physically integrate sources that must be combined to be understood; the effect is strong only when element interactivity is high.

essay.q: Present the three kinds of cognitive load and their additivity, with one programming example for each.
essay.m: Hint: Intrinsic: from element interactivity and prior knowledge (recursion needs call, argument, base case, stack held together). Extraneous: from presentation or needless activity (diagram and explanation on separate pages, vague task text). Germane: effort to build schemas (self-explaining an example, comparing two solutions). Intrinsic and extraneous are additive; germane load may be raised only while the total stays within working-memory limits (Sweller 1998).

essay.q: Explain why means-ends analysis hinders learning per Sweller (1988), citing at least two pieces of evidence.
essay.m: Hint: Means-ends requires holding the current state, goal, differences, operators and subgoals; that leaves little capacity for schemas. Evidence: the production-system model (4 productions vs 1, 5 cycles vs 3, 29 vs 17 conditions matched), Owen and Sweller 1985 (the conventional group made 4 to 6 times as many mathematical errors per side), the dual-task experiment with 24 Year-10 students (the goal-free group made fewer reproduction errors), Sweller, Mawer and Ward 1983.

essay.q: Compare worked examples, completion problems and goal-free problems: how each reduces load, its limits, and when to use it.
essay.m: Hint: All three avoid means-ends. Worked example: strong for novices; limits: motivation and stereotyped patterns, and split-attention formats destroy the effect. Completion: forces study of the partial solution and sustains long-term motivation; limit: costly to design. Goal-free: turns the question into "calculate as many variables as you can"; limit: fits maths and science where state spaces are small. Use the completion strategy to fade support.

essay.q: Present expertise reversal and how to design for students of different levels in introductory programming.
essay.m: Hint: The worked-example effect disappears then reverses as learners become skilled (Kalyuga 2001, 2003; Kirschner 2006). Practice: measure prior knowledge with a pretest; weaker students get worked examples and step-by-step hints; stronger ones get completion tasks then blank tasks; fade the AI's guidance; test for a level × method interaction in the analysis.

essay.q: Analyze the argument of Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006) and name two points open to rebuttal (use Module 01 too).
essay.m: Hint: Argument: minimal guidance ignores working-memory limits; controlled evidence favours strong guidance for novices; the advantage of guidance shrinks as prior knowledge grows. Rebuttals (Kapur 2016): CLT assumes no prior knowledge; the fair comparison is with "solve first, then teach"; high load is not always bad; Mayer 2004 supports guided discovery. Also, the PBL studies from medicine are a narrow context.

essay.q: Propose ways to measure cognitive load in your study, giving pros and cons of each.
essay.m: Hint: 9-point subjective scale (Paas 1992): sensitive, reliable, non-intrusive but self-reported. Physiological measures: more objective but less reliable and sensitive only to large differences (Paas et al. 1994). Secondary tasks: a direct indicator but interfere with the main task. Combine effort and performance via z-scores (Paas and van Merriënboer 1993) to compute instructional efficiency between treatment and control.

essay.q: Explain the variability effect and the transfer paradox, then state the implication for sequencing programming exercises.
essay.m: Hint: Variability in practice helps transfer but raises load during learning (the transfer paradox). CLT reading: it helps only when extraneous load is low (worked examples), because germane load rises while the total stays within limits (Paas and van Merriënboer 1994a). Implication: use load-reducing formats (worked examples, completion) combined with a random order of problem types (different surface, same structure), not only an easy-to-hard order.
